To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the tag+ and tag+ genes of E. coli encode the 3-methyl adenine DNA glycosases I and II and that high expression of the tag gene product suppresses the alkA mutant phenotype and that high expression alkA+ gene product greatly increases the alkylating agent sensitivity of the wild type.

the tag+ and the alkA+ genes were cloned and expressed in E. coli and that the tag+ coded protein, 3-methyl adenine glycosylase, is a 21 kDa protein and is responsible for the repair of DNA damage caused by alkylation.
the tag and alk genes of E. coli are cloned, expressed, and characterized as 3-methyl adenine DNA glycosyases I and II.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cloning of genes which code for proteins that are involved in the repair of DNA damage.
the isolation of genes involved in DNA repair and the identification of their gene products.
the cloning and expression of genes involved in the repair of alkylating agent-induced DNA damage in E. coli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the alkA+-encoded 3-methyladennine DNA glycoslase II plays an essential role in the repair of alkylating agent-damaged DNA.

the tag+ and the alkA+ genes code for the two 3-methyl adenine DNA glycosyles of E. coli, that the two enzymes have different roles in DNA repair, and that the tag+ gene product can be overproduced to a level which is sufficient to replace the alkA+-encoded 3-methyl-adenine glycosylase in DNA repair.
overexpression of tag+ and alk+ in E. coli leads to a high level of 3-methlyadenine-DNA-glycosylase I and II.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

overproduction of the tag+- or alkA+-coded DNA glycosylasessuppresses the alkylation resistance of alkA mutants and that overproduction of 3-methyadenine DNA glycolase II greatly sensitizes wildtype E. coli cells to alkylnitrosourea.
the tag+- and alkA+-coded enzymes can be expressed at high levels without affecting the viability of the cell and that the tag+-coded enzyme is a more efficient DNA repair glycosylase.
the tag+ and the alkA+ genes encode the 3-methyl adenine DNA glycosy-lases I and II, respectively, and that the expression of these genes can be controlled by a variety of means.
The main takeaway from our work is that
overproduction of the E. coli tag+ gene product, 3-methyl adenine DNA glycosase I (TAG), can almost completely suppress the alkylation sensitivities of alkA mutants.
the alkA gene product may be an alkyltransferase.
overproduction of the tag+- and alkA+-coded enzymes can be used to study the biological role of these enzymes in DNA repair.
